newsitem.title: FRANCE: French govt seen studying corporate tax rise.
newsitem.headline: French govt seen studying corporate tax rise.

text.p: France's Socialist-led government is studying an increase in corporate tax to help bring down the public deficit, a source close to the government said on Thursday.

Under the plan, corporate tax could be raised to around 40 percent of profits from its current level of 36.6 percent, a level which includes a special 10 percent increase imposed by the previous centre-right government.

Small and medium sized companies, seen as the country's engines of jobs creation, would be exempt from this measure and the increase would be structured in such a way as to avoid harming investment, the source added.
Other plans under consideration include a rise in company social security contributions, and increased taxes on savings that would affect well-off households.
French daily Le Figaro said on Thursday the government might consider raising taxes on life insurance policies, but the source said no decision had been made on this.

The government may also seek contributions from state-owned companies, the source said. French governments have traditionally tapped state bank Caisse des Depots et Consignations to plug holes in the budget.
The government is also studying some savings measures.
Government spokeswoman Catherine Trautmann said after a special ministerial meeting on Thursday that no final decisions had been made on how to tackle the expected 1997 budget deficit.

She said the decisions would be taken after the submission on Monday of an audit of public finances, which the source said was likely to show a deficit of 3.5 to 3.6 percent of gross domestic product.
The source said the deficit was primarily due to revenue shortfalls and that government measures to cut the gap were mostly aimed at boosting revenues rather than cutting spending.
He said the government was seeking to avoid anything that would deter consumption in France.
